overview.text: Acts describes the gift of the Holy Spirit, Peter’s preaching, Baptism, and the common life of the first believers. The calendar year is approximate.

readings.title: The life of the first believers
readings.text: And they continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers. 43 And fear came upon every soul: and many wonders and signs were done by the apostles. 44 And all that believed were together, and had all things common; 45 And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need. 46 And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart, 47 Praising God, and having favour with all the people. And the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved.

readings.title: OCA history: Christ and the Apostles

overview.text: The apostles and elders consider Gentile converts and circumcision. Their letter does not impose the full Mosaic ceremonial law on Gentiles. The date is approximate.

readings.title: The council’s letter
readings.text: For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things; 29 That ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication: from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well. Fare ye well.

events.title: Ignatius of Antioch: bishop and Eucharist

overview.text: In his letter to Smyrna, Ignatius links the local church’s unity, its bishop, and the celebration of the Eucharist. This is an early second-century witness; the date is approximate.

readings.title: Bishop, presbyters, deacons, and Eucharist
readings.text: See that you all follow the bishop, even as Jesus Christ does the Father, and the presbytery as you would the apostles; and reverence the deacons, as being the institution of God. Let no man do anything connected with the Church without the bishop. Let that be deemed a proper Eucharist, which is [administered] either by the bishop, or by one to whom he has entrusted it. Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church. It is not lawful without the bishop either to baptize or to celebrate a love-feast; but whatsoever he shall approve of, that is also pleasing to God, so that everything that is done may be secure and valid.

overview.text: Against Gnostic claims to secret teaching, Irenaeus appeals to the publicly transmitted faith and succession of bishops in the churches. The position on the year axis is approximate.

readings.title: Apostolic tradition in the churches
readings.text: It is within the power of all, therefore, in every Church, who may wish to see the truth, to contemplate clearly the tradition of the apostles manifested throughout the whole world; and we are in a position to reckon up those who were by the apostles instituted bishops in the Churches, and [to demonstrate] the succession of these men to our own times; those who neither taught nor knew of anything like what these [heretics] rave about.

readings.title: OCA history: Irenaeus and the biblical canon

overview.text: Constantine and Licinius grant Christians freedom of worship and restoration of confiscated property. Christianity’s legalization changes its public circumstances; it does not make Christianity the empire’s sole official religion in 313.

readings.title: OCA history: Constantine and religious toleration

overview.text: The council rejects Arius’s teaching that the Son is a creature and confesses the Son as of one substance with the Father. It also issues disciplinary canons.

readings.title: The Nicene Creed of 325
readings.text: We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the only-begotten of his Father, of the substance of the Father, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten (γεννηθέντα), not made, being of one substance (ὁμοούσιον, consubstantialem) with the Father. By whom all things were made, both which be in heaven and in earth. Who for us men and for our salvation came down [from heaven] and was incarnate and was made man. He suffered and the third day he rose again, and ascended into heaven. And he shall come again to judge both the quick and the dead. And [we believe] in the Holy Ghost. And whosoever shall say that there was a time when the Son of God was not (ἤν ποτε ὅτε οὐκ ἦν), or that before he was begotten he was not, or that he was made of things that were not, or that he is of a different substance or essence [from the Father] or that he is a creature, or subject to change or conversion [τρεπτὸν in Greek; convertibilem in Latin] — all that so say, the Catholic and Apostolic Church anathematizes them.

readings.title: OCA history: the First Ecumenical Council

events.title: Athanasius lists the New Testament books

overview.text: Athanasius’s thirty-ninth Festal Letter lists the twenty-seven books of the New Testament. His letter is a dated witness within the longer reception of the biblical canon, rather than a decree of Nicaea.

readings.title: The New Testament list
readings.text: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John.

readings.title: Read the whole letter, including its Old Testament list

overview.text: The council reaffirms Nicaea and condemns teachings denying the Holy Spirit’s divinity. The creed received under this council’s name confesses the Spirit as Lord and giver of life, worshipped with the Father and Son.

readings.title: The Holy Spirit and the Church
readings.text: And [we believe] in the Holy Ghost, the Lord and Giver-of-Life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified, who spoke by the prophets. And [we believe] in one, holy, (II) Catholic and Apostolic Church. We acknowledge one Baptism for the remission of sins, [and] we look for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. Amen.

readings.title: OCA history: the Second Ecumenical Council

events.title: Ephesus · Third Ecumenical Council

overview.text: The council condemns Nestorius and approves Cyril’s teaching on the unity of the incarnate Word. Calling Mary Theotokos safeguards the confession that the one born from her is God the Word made flesh.

events.rulingLabel: Approval of Cyril’s second letter to Nestorius

readings.title: Why the title Mother of God is used
readings.locator: Cyril’s second letter to Nestorius, read and approved at the council
readings.text: This was the sentiment of the holy Fathers; therefore they ventured to call the Holy Virgin, the Mother of God, not as if the nature of the Word or his divinity had its beginning from the Holy Virgin, but because of her was born that holy body with a rational soul, to which the Word being personally united is said to be born according to the flesh.

readings.title: OCA history: the Third Ecumenical Council

overview.text: The definition confesses one and the same Christ in two natures, fully divine and fully human. Its reception is disputed, contributing to the enduring separation between the Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian churches.

readings.title: The Definition of Faith
readings.text: Following the holy Fathers we teach with one voice that the Son [of God] and our Lord Jesus Christ is to be confessed as one and the same [Person], that he is perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, very God and very man, of a reasonable soul and [human] body consisting, consubstantial with the Father as touching his Godhead, and consubstantial with us as touching his manhood; made in all things like us, sin only excepted; begotten of his Father before the worlds according to his Godhead; but in these last days for us men and for our salvation born [into the world] of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of God according to his manhood. This one and the same Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son [of God] must be confessed to be in two natures, unconfusedly, immutably, indivisibly, inseparably [united], and that without the distinction of natures being taken away by such union, but rather the peculiar property of each nature being preserved and being united in one Person and subsistence, not separated or divided into two persons, but one and the same Son and only-begotten, God the Word, our Lord Jesus Christ, as the Prophets of old time have spoken concerning him, and as the Lord Jesus Christ has taught us, and as the Creed of the Fathers has delivered to us.

readings.title: OCA history: the Fourth Ecumenical Council
OCA history: the Oriental Orthodox Churches

developments.text: The Oriental Orthodox churches are distinct from Eastern Orthodoxy. The separation concerns the reception of Chalcedon and its Christological language; it should not be described as the origin of Protestantism.

events.title: Constantinople II · Fifth Ecumenical Council

overview.text: The council condemns the Three Chapters and interprets Chalcedon in continuity with Cyril. It insists that Christ’s divine and human acts belong to the same incarnate Word, one of the Holy Trinity.

events.rulingLabel: Fourteen Capitula; condemnation of the Three Chapters

readings.title: The crucified Christ is one of the Trinity
readings.text: If anyone does not confess that our Lord Jesus Christ who was crucified in the flesh is true God and the Lord of Glory and one of the Holy Trinity: let him be anathema.

readings.title: The same Christ acts and suffers
readings.text: If anyone shall say that the wonder-working Word of God is one [Person] and the Christ that suffered another; or shall say that God the Word was with the woman-born Christ, or was in him as one person in another, but that he was not one and the same our Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God, incarnate and made man, and that his miracles and the sufferings which of his own will he endured in the flesh were not of the same [Person]: let him be anathema.

readings.title: OCA history: the Fifth Ecumenical Council

overview.text: Against Monothelitism, the council confesses two natural wills and two natural operations in the one Christ. His human will is preserved and freely follows his divine will.

readings.title: Two natural wills in the one Christ
readings.text: defining all this we likewise declare that in him are two natural wills and two natural operations indivisibly, inconvertibly, inseparably, inconfusedly, according to the teaching of the holy Fathers. And these two natural wills are not contrary the one to the other (God forbid!) as the impious heretics assert, but his human will follows and that not as resisting and reluctant, but rather as subject to his divine and omnipotent will.

readings.title: OCA history: the Sixth Ecumenical Council

overview.text: This council issues disciplinary canons to supplement the fifth and sixth councils. Eastern Orthodoxy receives its canons; their reception in Rome is contested. It does not issue another Christological definition comparable to the seven ecumenical councils.

readings.title: Continuity of the faith
readings.text: That order is best of all which makes every word and act begin and end in God. Wherefore that piety may be clearly set forth by us and that the Church of which Christ is the foundation may be continually increased and advanced, and that it may be exalted above the cedars of Lebanon; now therefore we, by divine grace at the beginning of our decrees, define that the faith set forth by the God-chosen Apostles who themselves had both seen and were ministers of the Word, shall be preserved without any innovation, unchanged and inviolate.

readings.title: OCA history: Trullo and its reception

overview.text: Imperial opposition to icons provokes prolonged conflict. Defenders connect sacred images to the reality of the Incarnation. Nicaea II’s decision in 787 is followed by a second period of iconoclasm before the restoration of 843.

readings.title: OCA history: the end of iconoclasm

events.title: Nicaea II · Seventh Ecumenical Council

overview.text: The council restores the veneration of holy icons and distinguishes this honor from the worship belonging to God alone. Honor given to an image passes to the person represented.

events.rulingLabel: Definition of Faith on holy images

readings.title: Veneration and worship are distinguished
readings.text: For by so much more frequently as they are seen in artistic representation, by so much more readily are men lifted up to the memory of their prototypes, and to a longing after them; and to these should be given due salutation and honourable reverence (ἀσπασμὸν καὶ τιμητικὴν προσκύνησιν), not indeed that true worship of faith (λατρείαν) which pertains alone to the divine nature; but to these, as to the figure of the precious and life-giving Cross and to the Book of the Gospels and to the other holy objects, incense and lights may be offered according to ancient pious custom. For the honour which is paid to the image passes on to that which the image represents, and he who reveres the image reveres in it the subject represented.

readings.title: Read the complete Definition and proceedings

events.title: Restoration of icons · Triumph of Orthodoxy

overview.text: Under Empress Theodora and Patriarch Methodius, icons are restored after the second iconoclast period. Eastern Orthodoxy commemorates this restoration on the first Sunday of Great Lent.

events.rulingLabel: Restoration of the decisions of Nicaea II

readings.title: OCA history: the restoration of icons

overview.text: Forged papal letters and related collections circulated under ancient authorities. The MGH edition places their substantial completion around 847–852 in the province of Reims. Their protections for bishops and later use in canon law must be distinguished from their false attribution.

readings.title: Read the critical-edition overview (German)
readings.locator: Overview: composition, purposes, and later reception

developments.text: The Donation of Constantine was a separate forgery incorporated into the Pseudo-Isidorian collection. Valla later challenged that document; his argument did not establish that every medieval papal claim originated in forgery.

overview.text: The brothers arrive in Moravia and develop Christian teaching and worship in Slavonic. Their disciples later carry this work into Bulgaria. Their mission involves both Constantinople and Rome before the later East–West separation.

readings.title: OCA history: Cyril, Methodius, and the Slavic mission

overview.text: A council in Constantinople restores communion involving Patriarch Photius and Roman representatives and reaffirms the unaltered Creed. Orthodox reception esteems this council; its ecumenical numbering is not universally agreed.

readings.title: OCA history: Photius, the councils, and the Creed

overview.text: Prince Vladimir receives Baptism and promotes the Christianization of Kievan Rus, receiving bishops and clergy from Byzantium. This is a major stage in the history inherited by the Russian Church.

readings.title: OCA history: Saint Vladimir of Kiev

events.title: Filioque enters the Roman liturgical Creed

overview.text: John Paul II’s historical account dates the addition of the Filioque to Rome’s Creed to Henry II’s coronation in 1014. Earlier Latin use preceded Rome’s adoption. The Catholic catechism acknowledges continuing Orthodox disagreement over its introduction into the Creed.

events.rulingLabel: Roman liturgical adoption of the Filioque

readings.title: Catholic acknowledgement of the continuing dispute
readings.text: a point of disagreement with the Orthodox Churches.

overview.text: Roman legates and the Constantinopolitan synod exchange personal excommunications amid accumulated disputes. The date marks a stage in a prolonged estrangement; it is not a single act that instantly separated every Eastern and Western Christian.

readings.title: Joint declaration explaining the scope of the 1054 censures

developments.text: The Fourth Crusade intensifies the separation in 1204. In 1965, Rome and Constantinople remove the 1054 censures from memory; their declaration does not establish full ecclesiastical communion.

events.title: Dictatus Papae and Gregorian papal claims

overview.text: Twenty-seven propositions in Gregory VII’s register articulate extensive papal authority. The manuscript position is dated 1075; authorship and intended use require care. The text is evidence of Gregorian claims, rather than a universally received ecumenical ruling.

readings.title: Claims about the Roman see and episcopal authority
readings.text: That the Roman church was founded by God alone. That the Roman pontiff alone can with right be called universal. That he alone can depose or reinstate bishops.

readings.title: Claim about emperors
readings.text: That it may be permitted to him to depose emperors.

readings.title: Claim about judgment of the pope
readings.text: That he himself may be judged by no one.

overview.text: Henry V renounced investiture by ring and staff, while Calixtus II allowed a regulated imperial role in German episcopal elections and temporal regalia. The agreement distinguished consecration from political possession in a negotiated settlement of the investiture conflict.

readings.title: Henry V renounces investiture by ring and staff
readings.text: In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, I, Henry, by the grace of God august emperor of the Romans, for the love of God and of the holy Roman church and of our master pope Calixtus, and for the healing of my soul, do remit to God, and to the holy apostles of God, Peter and Paul, and to the holy catholic church, all investiture through ring and staff; and do grant that in all the churches that are in my kingdom or empire there may be canonical election and free consecration.

readings.title: Read both sides of the agreement

overview.text: Crusaders sack Constantinople, plunder churches, and establish Latin rule and a Latin patriarch. The destruction deepens the estrangement between Greek Christians and the Latin West.

developments.text: Byzantine rulers recover Constantinople in 1261, after fifty-seven years of Latin rule. The later union agreement at Florence in 1439 attempts to resolve the continuing separation.

overview.text: The Western council’s confession described Eucharistic change of substance. Its disciplinary constitutions required annual confession and Easter communion, regulated clergy and education, and asserted Roman ecclesiastical order. These are Latin conciliar decisions, not a council received as ecumenical by the Orthodox Church.

readings.title: Eucharistic language
readings.text: the bread and wine having been changed in substance, by God’s power, into his body and blood

readings.title: Read the confession and disciplinary constitutions
readings.locator: Constitution 1: Confession of Faith; constitution 21: annual confession

overview.text: Aquinas began the Summa in 1265 and left it unfinished. Its disputed-question method distinguishes philosophical reasoning from revealed sacred doctrine. Reading Aquinas’s own account supplies context for later Orthodox criticism of scholastic theology without reducing his position to reason alone.

readings.title: Why Aquinas distinguishes revelation from philosophy
readings.text: I answer that, It was necessary for man's salvation that there should be a knowledge revealed by God besides philosophical science built up by human reason. Firstly, indeed, because man is directed to God, as to an end that surpasses the grasp of his reason: "The eye hath not seen, O God, besides Thee, what things Thou hast prepared for them that wait for Thee" (Isaiah 64:4). But the end must first be known by men who are to direct their thoughts and actions to the end. Hence it was necessary for the salvation of man that certain truths which exceed human reason should be made known to him by divine revelation.

readings.title: Read the whole question on sacred doctrine

events.title: Second Council of Lyons

overview.text: At Lyons the Latin council restated the procession of the Spirit from Father and Son as one principle. A union with Byzantine representatives was proclaimed. Its decree records the Latin doctrinal position; proclamation of union did not secure enduring East–West communion.

events.rulingLabel: Constitution on the procession of the Holy Spirit

readings.title: The Latin formula of procession
readings.text: the holy Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son, not as from two principles, but as from one principle

readings.title: Read the council’s constitutions and union context

overview.text: In conflict with royal power, Boniface VIII asserted one Church, the subordination of temporal power to spiritual power, and the necessity of subjection to the Roman pontiff. The bull is a primary statement of medieval papal claims, not an Orthodox ecclesiological definition.

readings.title: The bull’s concluding definition
readings.text: Furthermore, we declare, we proclaim, we define that it is absolutely necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff.

readings.title: Read the whole bull
readings.locator: Church unity, the two swords, and Roman authority

overview.text: Councils in Constantinople defend Gregory Palamas’s account of participation in God’s uncreated energies while God’s essence remains inaccessible. These are later Orthodox synods, not additional councils within the traditional list of seven ecumenical councils.

readings.title: OCA history: Palamas, Barlaam, and the councils

events.title: Western Schism

overview.text: Rival Roman and Avignon papal obediences divided Latin Christianity after the disputed election of 1378. Pisa’s attempted settlement in 1409 added another claimant. Constance eventually ended the competing obediences and elected Martin V in 1417.

events.rulingLabel: Rival papal obediences; settlement at Constance

readings.title: Read the Constance decrees and historical introduction

events.title: Council of Constance and conciliarism

overview.text: Constance addressed the Western Schism, condemned Wyclif and Hus, and elected Martin V. Haec Sancta asserted conciliar authority over even papal dignity. Its authority and the ecumenical status of early sessions remain disputed within Catholic accounts; later papal doctrine did not adopt unrestricted conciliar supremacy.

events.rulingLabel: Haec Sancta, 6 April 1415; election of Martin V, 11 November 1417

readings.title: The conciliar claim
readings.text: has power immediately from Christ, and that everyone of whatever state or dignity, even papal, is bound to obey it

events.title: Florence proclaims union with the Greeks

overview.text: Laetentur caeli addressed the Filioque, Eucharistic bread, purification after death, and Roman primacy. Most Greek delegates signed; Mark of Ephesus declined. The decree did not secure lasting general Orthodox reception.

readings.title: The decree’s claim about Roman primacy
readings.locator: Decree of union with the Greeks
readings.text: the holy apostolic see and the Roman pontiff holds the primacy over the whole world

readings.title: Read the decree’s complete definitions
readings.locator: Session 6, 6 July 1439: union with the Greeks

events.title: Valla challenges the Donation of Constantine

overview.text: Lorenzo Valla composed a historical and linguistic attack on the Donation of Constantine, exposing its claim to fourth-century origin as false. Coleman’s edition dates the work to 1440 and its first printing to 1517. This was criticism within the Latin world before the Reformation.

events.rulingLabel: Discourse on the Forgery of the Alleged Donation of Constantine

readings.title: Valla states what he intends to prove
readings.text: For, as I shall show, that Donation whence the supreme pontiffs will have their right derived was unknown equally to Sylvester and to Constantine. But before I come to the refutation of the instrument of the Donation, which is their one defense, not only false but even stupid, the right order demands that I go further back.

readings.title: Read the editor’s historical introduction
readings.locator: Printed pp.1–8; composition and publication dates

developments.text: Coleman notes that Nicholas of Cusa had already questioned the document and that Valla’s work was first printed by Ulrich von Hutten in 1517. Their historical criticism belongs to the background of later disputes over papal authority.

overview.text: Ottoman forces capture Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire. Orthodox church life continues under changed political conditions. This is a political watershed, rather than a new doctrinal ruling.

readings.title: OCA history: the fall of Byzantium

overview.text: Under Patriarch Symeon, the Constantinopolitan synod rejects the union of Ferrara–Florence in 1482. A further session in 1484 issues a rite for receiving Latin converts by renunciation and Chrismation.

readings.title: George Dragas: the 1482 and 1484 synodal actions

developments.text: This historical reception rite belongs to a particular synodal context. It is not presented here as an instruction for a reader’s reception into the Church.

events.title: Fifth Lateran Council

overview.text: The council opposed a rival council at Pisa and legislated on ecclesiastical reform, preaching, printing, and theological teaching. It closed in March 1517. Its decrees document Catholic reform efforts before Luther’s theses, alongside continuing conflicts over councils and papal government.

events.rulingLabel: Fifth Lateran Council: reform, preaching, and printing decrees

readings.title: Read the council’s constitutions
readings.locator: Sessions 8–12; decrees on printing and preaching

overview.text: Luther circulated theses disputing indulgence preaching and papal authority over penalties. This marks a conventional starting point for the Reformation, rather than the founding of a fully developed Lutheran denomination.

readings.title: Thesis 1
readings.text: Our Lord and Master Jesus Christ in saying: "Repent ye," [12] etc., intended that the whole life of believers should be penitence.

developments.text: The controversy began within Western Latin Christianity. It was not a sixteenth-century secession from an Eastern Orthodox jurisdiction.

overview.text: To the Christian Nobility, The Babylonian Captivity of the Church, and The Freedom of a Christian extended the dispute into ecclesiastical authority, sacraments, faith, and Christian life.

readings.title: The Freedom of a Christian
readings.text: A Christian man is the most free lord of all, and subject to none; a Christian man is the most dutiful servant of all, and subject to every one.

readings.title: The three works in their historical English edition

events.title: Luther at the Diet of Worms

overview.text: After his excommunication, Luther appeared before the imperial Diet and refused to recant his writings. The Edict of Worms outlawed him; protection at the Wartburg allowed his work to continue.
Luther translated the New Testament at the Wartburg; the September Testament appeared in 1522. A first edition of his complete German Bible followed in 1534.

The first Zurich disputation placed Zwingli’s Sixty-Seven Articles before the city council. Swiss reform developed alongside the Lutheran movement, with differences that would become especially visible over the Eucharist.

readings.title: Article 1: Gospel and church authority
readings.locator: Sixty-Seven Articles, article 1; English text in the 1901 collection
readings.text: All who say that the Gospel is invalid without the confirmation of the Church err and slander God.

overview.text: Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz, and George Blaurock participated in believers’ baptisms in Zurich. This is a major beginning of Swiss Anabaptism; the wider Anabaptist movement had several regional beginnings.

readings.title: Swiss beginnings and later Baptist distinctions
Swiss Brethren and the confession of 1527

developments.text: Swiss Brethren rejected infant baptism and the reformers’ alliance with civic power. Later Baptist affinity does not establish one continuous organization from Zurich to every Baptist church.

overview.text: Swiss Brethren adopted seven articles addressing baptism, the ban, breaking bread, separation, pastors, the sword, and oaths. The confession expresses a particular Anabaptist stream rather than a universal Protestant position.

readings.title: Article I: opening clause on baptism
readings.locator: Schleitheim Articles I, opening clause; Estep source-book translation, 1976
readings.text: Baptism shall be given to all who have learned repentance and amendment of life,

events.title: Marburg: disagreement over the Lord’s Supper

overview.text: Luther and Zwingli met at Marburg. Their substantial agreement did not resolve whether Christ’s body and blood are bodily present in the Supper; the disagreement obstructed a united evangelical alliance.

readings.title: A Lutheran eyewitness’s report
readings.locator: October 1529; a partisan primary witness, not a neutral transcript

developments.text: Lutheran and Reformed Eucharistic teaching must be read separately. The shared label Protestant does not imply a single doctrine of the sacraments.

overview.text: Evangelical princes and cities protested the second Diet of Speyer’s religious policy. The resulting name Protestant came to cover several movements with differing confessions and church structures.

Melanchthon presented the Lutheran confession at the imperial Diet. Its teaching on justification and the Lord’s Supper is a confessional reference point for Lutheran churches and differs from later Reformed formulations.

readings.title: Article IV: justification
readings.locator: Augsburg Confession IV; historic Krauth English translation in Schaff
readings.text: Also they teach that men can not be justified [obtain forgiveness of sins and righteousness] before God by their own powers, merits, or works; but are justified freely [of grace] for Christ's sake through faith, when they believe that they are received into favor, and their sins forgiven for Christ's sake, who by his death hath satisfied for our sins.

readings.title: Article X: the Lord’s Supper
readings.locator: Augsburg Confession X; historic Krauth English translation in Schaff
readings.text: Of the Supper of the Lord they teach that the [true] body and blood of Christ are truly present [under the form of bread and wine], and are [there] communicated to those that eat in the Lord's Supper [and receive]. And they disapprove of those that teach otherwise [wherefore also the opposite doctrine is rejected].

overview.text: Parliament recognized Henry VIII as supreme head of the Church of England, rejecting papal jurisdiction. Later reigns brought major doctrinal and liturgical changes; the 1534 jurisdictional break alone did not settle Anglican theology.

readings.title: Parliament’s account of the English Reformation

overview.text: Swiss delegates meeting at Basel produced a shared confession. This early Helvetic agreement preceded Bullinger’s more widely received Second Helvetic Confession by thirty years.

readings.title: Article 2: interpretation of Scripture
readings.locator: First Helvetic Confession, article 2; Peter Chapman translation, CC BY 4.0
readings.text: The interpretation of Scripture is to be sought from itself alone, so that it should be its own interpreter, governed by the rule of love and faith.

readings.title: Historic text and editorial introduction
readings.locator: Confessio Helvetica Prior; Latin and German in Schaff

overview.text: The first edition of Calvin’s Institutes appeared at Basel. He repeatedly enlarged the work, reaching its major final Latin edition in 1559; later Reformed churches were not simply founded by this single publication.

readings.title: Calvin, the Institutes, and Reformed church formation

events.title: Papal approval of the Society of Jesus

overview.text: Paul III approved the Society of Jesus through Regimini militantis Ecclesiae on 27 September 1540. The Jesuits’ official history identifies this as the order’s foundation by papal approval. The institution became part of Catholic renewal, education, and mission during the Reformation era.

readings.title: Read the Society’s account of papal approval

overview.text: After returning to Geneva, Calvin helped establish ordinances for ministers, teachers, elders, deacons, worship, and discipline. The consistory became a defining feature of Genevan church government.

events.title: Council of Trent

overview.text: In three periods between 1545 and 1563, Trent defined Catholic teaching amid Reformation controversy and enacted reforms. Its decrees addressed Scripture and traditions, justification, and the sacraments. These Latin definitions answer Protestant claims while remaining distinct from Orthodox conciliar teaching.

events.rulingLabel: Sessions IV (1546), VI (1547), XIII (1551), and later decrees

readings.title: Scripture and apostolic traditions
readings.locator: Session IV, decree concerning the canonical Scriptures
readings.text: and seeing clearly that this truth and discipline are contained in the written books, and the unwritten traditions which, received by the Apostles from the mouth of Christ himself, or from the Apostles themselves, the Holy Ghost dictating, have come down even unto us, transmitted as it were from hand to hand; (the Synod) following the examples of the orthodox Fathers, receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety, and reverence, all the books both of the Old and of the New Testament--seeing that one God is the author of both --as also the said traditions, as well those appertaining to faith as to morals, as having been dictated, either by Christ's own word of mouth, or by the Holy Ghost, and preserved in the Catholic Church by a continuous succession.

readings.title: Justification includes renewal and is received by grace
readings.text: This disposition, or preparation, is followed by Justification itself, which is not remission of sins merely, but also the sanctification and renewal of the inward man, through the voluntary reception of the grace, and of the gifts, whereby man of unjust becomes just, and of an enemy a friend, that so he may be an heir according to hope of life everlasting.

readings.title: Trent denies that prior works merit justification
readings.text: but we are therefore said to be justified freely, because that none of those things which precede justification-whether faith or works-merit the grace itself of justification. For, if it be a grace, it is not now by works, otherwise, as the same Apostle says, grace is no more grace.

readings.title: The Eucharistic conversion
readings.text: And because that Christ, our Redeemer, declared that which He offered under the species of bread to be truly His own body, therefore has it ever been a firm belief in the Church of God, and this holy Synod doth now declare it anew, that, by the consecration of the bread and of the wine, a conversion is made of the whole substance of the bread into the substance of the body of Christ our Lord, and of the whole substance of the wine into the substance of His blood; which conversion is, by the holy Catholic Church, suitably and properly called Transubstantiation.

readings.title: Read all Trent sessions
readings.locator: Waterworth’s 1848 edition: contents and session links

events.title: The first Book of Common Prayer

overview.text: Under Edward VI, Parliament prescribed the first English Book of Common Prayer. Revisions in 1552, 1559, and 1662 show that Anglican worship developed through several settlements rather than one unchanging Reformation text.

readings.title: The Reformation and the Prayer Book

overview.text: The imperial settlement recognized Roman Catholicism and the Augsburg Confession within its legal arrangements. It did not grant equivalent recognition to Reformed Christians or establish modern freedom of religion for every individual.

The Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity restored royal supremacy and required a revised Prayer Book after Mary I’s Catholic restoration. The settlement retained bishops while placing the English church within the Reformation.

The first national synod of French Reformed churches adopted a confession associated with Calvin and his colleagues. Its articles articulate Reformed views of Scripture, church discipline, sacraments, and church government amid persecution.

readings.title: Article XXXIII: human laws and conscience
readings.locator: French Confession XXXIII; Schaff historical English translation
readings.text: However, we reject all human inventions, and all laws which men may introduce under the pretense of serving God, by which they wish to bind consciences ; and we receive only that which conduces to concord and holds all in obedience, from the greatest to the least.

overview.text: The Scottish Parliament adopted the confession drafted by Knox and five colleagues. Reformed doctrine and subsequent Presbyterian organization developed in Scotland; Westminster later replaced this confession as the principal Scottish doctrinal standard.

readings.title: Article XVIII: how the true church is identified
readings.locator: Scots Confession XVIII, opening statement of criteria; original Scots wording retained
readings.text: The notes, signes, and assured takens whereby the immaculate Spouse of Christ Jesus is knawen fra the horrible harlot, the Kirk malignant, we affirme, are nouther Antiquitie, Title usurpit, lineal Descence, Place appointed, nor multitude of men approving ane error.

readings.title: Read the Scots Confession in its historic wording
readings.locator: Articles I–XXV; Scots and Latin in Schaff

overview.text: Guido de Brès prepared this confession for Reformed believers in the Low Countries. Its reception helped establish a confessional identity later joined with Heidelberg and the Canons of Dort as the Three Forms of Unity.

readings.title: Article VII: sufficiency of Scripture
readings.locator: Belgic Confession VII; uninterrupted English excerpt in Schaff
readings.text: For since the whole manner of worship which God requires of us is written in them at large, it is unlawful for any one, though an Apostle, to teach otherwise than we are now taught in the Holy Scriptures: nay, though it were an angel from heaven, as the Apostle Paul saith. For since it is forbidden to add unto or take away any thing from the Word of God, it doth thereby evidently appear that the doctrine thereof is most perfect and complete in all respects.

overview.text: Commissioned in the Electoral Palatinate, Heidelberg teaches Christian faith through questions and answers arranged around guilt, grace, and gratitude. Its discussions of faith, good works, baptism, and the Supper remain central to many Reformed churches.

readings.title: Question 64: faith and its fruits
readings.locator: Heidelberg Catechism, answer 64; historical English translation in Schaff
readings.text: No; for it is impossible that those who are implanted into Christ by true faith should not bring forth fruits of righteousness.

readings.title: Read the complete catechism
readings.locator: Current CRC edition; questions 60–85 on faith, works, and sacraments

overview.text: Bullinger’s confession was published and received by Swiss and other Reformed churches. It treats Scripture, councils, salvation, the church, sacraments, worship, and civil government in an extensive doctrinal statement.

readings.title: Chapter I: Scripture
readings.locator: Appendix: English Second Helvetic Confession, chapter I; historic translation in Schaff
readings.text: We believe and confess the Canonical Scriptures of the holy prophets and apostles of both Testaments to be the true Word of God, and to have sufficient authority of themselves, not of men. For God himself spake to the fathers, prophets, apostles, and still speaks to us through the Holy Scriptures.

overview.text: The Articles developed from earlier Tudor formularies; the 1571 settlement made subscription a requirement for clergy. They provide an Anglican doctrinal standard alongside the Prayer Book and episcopal order.

readings.title: Article XIX: the visible church
readings.locator: Thirty-Nine Articles XIX; original 1571 English column in Schaff
readings.text: The visible Church of Christe, is a congregation of faythfull men in the which the pure worde of God is preached, and the Sacramentes be duely ministred, accordyng to Christes ordinaunce in all those thynges that of necessitie are requisite to the same.

readings.title: Articles VI, XI, XVII, and XXV–XXVIII

events.title: Jeremias II and the Tübingen Lutherans

overview.text: Lutheran theologians send the Augsburg Confession in Greek to Patriarch Jeremias II. Their correspondence tests proposed agreement and records substantial disagreements. The OCA account dates the main exchange to about 1575–1581.

events.rulingLabel: Responses of Patriarch Jeremias II to the Augsburg Confession

readings.title: OCA history: the correspondence and its theological issues

developments.text: The OCA history identifies differing approaches to the Church Fathers and biblical interpretation as central to the failed dialogue. This was an encounter between existing churches, not a Lutheran secession from Eastern Orthodoxy.

events.title: Formula and Book of Concord

overview.text: The Formula of Concord addressed disputes among Lutherans after Luther’s death. Its inclusion in the 1580 Book of Concord gathered several Lutheran confessional texts, without turning the collection into a Reformed confession.

events.rulingLabel: Formula of Concord; Book of Concord

readings.title: Original sin and human nature
readings.locator: Formula of Concord, Epitome I, affirmative thesis 1; Schaff English translation
readings.text: I. We believe, teach, and confess that there is a distinction between the nature of man itself, not only as man was created of God in the beginning pure and holy and free from sin, but also as we now possess it after our nature has fallen; a distinction, namely, between the nature itself, which even after the fall is and remains God's creature, and Original Sin; and that this difference between nature and Original Sin is as great as between the work of God and the work of the devil.

readings.title: The confessions and their dates
readings.locator: Formula of Concord, 1577; Book of Concord, 1580

events.title: Patriarchate of Moscow

overview.text: Patriarch Jeremias II recognizes Job as Patriarch of Moscow in 1589. Other Eastern patriarchs approve Moscow’s patriarchal status in 1593, placing it fifth in honor after the four ancient Eastern patriarchates.

events.rulingLabel: Establishment and recognition of the Moscow Patriarchate

readings.title: OCA history: establishment and recognition of the Moscow patriarchate

overview.text: Ruthenian bishops accept communion with Rome while retaining their Eastern rites. Many Orthodox clergy and faithful oppose the union, producing competing ecclesiastical allegiances in the region.

readings.title: OCA history: the Union of Brest-Litovsk

events.title: Smyth’s congregation and General Baptist beginnings

overview.text: An English Separatist congregation in Amsterdam adopted believers’ baptism under John Smyth. Helwys and others subsequently developed the English General Baptist stream, distinguished from later Particular Baptists by their understanding of Christ’s atonement.

readings.title: Smyth, Helwys, and General Baptist origins

developments.text: Baptist beginnings involve English Separatism and contact with continental believers’ baptism. They should not be collapsed into either a single Anabaptist succession or a uniform Calvinist origin.

events.title: The Five Articles of the Remonstrants

overview.text: Followers of Jacobus Arminius presented five articles to the Dutch authorities. Their account of election, atonement, grace, and perseverance became the immediate theological context of the Synod of Dort’s response.

readings.title: Article II: the extent of the atonement
readings.locator: Five Articles of the Remonstrants II; opening clause, historical English translation in Schaff
readings.text: That, agreeably thereto, Jesus Christ, the Saviour of the world, died for all men and for every man, so that he has obtained for them all, by his death on the cross, redemption and the forgiveness of sins; yet that no one actually enjoys this forgiveness of sins except the believer,

events.title: Helwys returns to England

overview.text: Helwys’s group established a General Baptist congregation in London. His Mystery of Iniquity argued for religious liberty beyond his own congregation, illustrating a Baptist approach to church and civil authority distinct from established national churches.

events.rulingLabel: A Short Declaration of the Mystery of Iniquity

readings.title: Helwys, the London congregation, and religious liberty

overview.text: An international Reformed synod rejected the Remonstrants’ positions and adopted the Canons of Dort. The canons address disputed points, not the whole of Reformed doctrine; their five headings are not a complete Protestant catechism.

readings.title: First head, article 7: election
readings.locator: Canons of Dort, first head of doctrine, article 7; historic English in Schaff
readings.text: Election is the unchangeable purpose of God, whereby, before the foundation of the world, he hath, out of mere grace, according to the sovereign good pleasure of his own will, chosen, from the whole human race, which had fallen through their own fault, from their primitive state of rectitude, into sin and destruction, a certain number of persons to redemption in Christ, whom he from eternity appointed the Mediator and head of the elect, and the foundation of salvation.

readings.title: Read all five heads and the rejection of errors

events.title: Calvinist confession published under Lucaris’s name

overview.text: A confession containing Calvinist teachings appears under Patriarch Cyril Lucaris’s name. Its authorship is disputed in the historical sources: the Synod of Jerusalem rejects the attribution while condemning the confession’s doctrines.

events.rulingLabel: The Eastern Confession of the Christian Faith (1629)

readings.title: Read the confession published under Lucaris’s name
The translator reports the synod’s position
readings.text: Thirdly. That the Confession of Cyril is not, as a matter of fact, that of the Church.

overview.text: London Separatist congregations produced the Particular Baptist stream during the 1630s. Their Calvinistic understanding of redemption distinguished them from General Baptists. Accounts distinguish an initial separation around 1633 from subsequent believers’ baptism in 1638.

events.title: Iași: revised Confession of Peter Mogila

overview.text: A council at Iași approves a modified version of Peter Mogila’s Confession of Faith. The OCA history also notes the influence of Latin scholastic forms on Mogila’s theological education and writings.

events.rulingLabel: Revised Orthodox Confession of Peter Mogila

readings.title: OCA history: Mogila, his schools, and the revised confession

overview.text: Seven London Particular Baptist congregations published a shared confession to explain their beliefs and answer accusations. Revisions followed in 1646 and 1651; the linked 2022 edition integrates material from those versions.

readings.title: Article 39: baptism, opening clause
readings.locator: Article 39.1, opening clause; Comprehensive Edition (2022), not an asserted facsimile of 1644
readings.text: Baptism is an ordinance of the New Testament, given by Christ [a] , to be dispensed upon persons professing faith,

readings.title: Read the confession with edition differences

overview.text: The Westminster Assembly completed its confession in 1646; the Church of Scotland adopted it in 1647. Its reception shaped Presbyterian standards, while Congregationalists and Particular Baptists later adapted its structure with important changes.

readings.title: Chapter I.6: Scripture and doctrinal deduction
readings.locator: Westminster Confession I.6; historical text in Schaff
readings.text: The whole counsel of God, concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man's salvation, faith, and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture: unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men.

readings.title: Chapters XI, XXVII–XXIX, XXX–XXXI
readings.locator: Justification, sacraments, church discipline, and councils

developments.text: Westminster, Savoy, and the Second London Baptist Confession share extensive text. Their differences over government and baptism identify distinct confessional traditions, rather than interchangeable churches.

overview.text: Congregational representatives adapted Westminster’s theology while setting out a different account of church government. The independence and authority of gathered congregations distinguish the declaration from Presbyterian polity.

readings.title: The power of a gathered church
readings.locator: Savoy Declaration: Of the Institution of Churches, and the Order Appointed in Them by Jesus Christ, paragraph IV
readings.text: To each of these Churches thus gathered, according unto his mind declared in his Word, he hath given all that Power and Authority which is any way needful for their carrying on that Order in Worship and Discipline which he hath instituted for them to observe with Commands and Rules for the due and right exerting and executing of that Power.

events.title: Moscow council and the Old Believer schism

overview.text: The Moscow council deposes Patriarch Nikon but upholds the liturgical reforms associated with him. It condemns resistance to the reforms; coercion and persecution deepen the division with the Old Believers.

readings.title: OCA history: Nikon, the council, and the Old Believers

events.title: Jerusalem/Bethlehem: Confession of Dositheus

overview.text: The synod under Patriarch Dositheus rejects the Calvinist confession attributed to Lucaris and adopts its own eighteen decrees. It addresses Scripture, predestination, justification, Church authority, and the sacraments. This is a later Orthodox synod, outside the seven-council list.

events.rulingLabel: Confession of Dositheus; eighteen decrees and four questions

readings.title: Justification, faith, and works
readings.text: We believe a man to be not simply justified through faith alone, but through faith which worketh through love, that is to say, through faith and works.

readings.title: Predestination is not without cause
readings.text: We believe the most good God to have from eternity predestinated unto glory those whom He hath chosen, and to have consigned unto condemnation those whom He hath rejected ; but not so that He would justify the one, and consign and condemn the other without cause.

readings.title: Read all eighteen decrees and the questions
OCA history: the confession in its seventeenth-century context

developments.text: The synod gives a direct historical Orthodox answer to Calvinist formulations. Its full text should be read with its seventeenth-century controversy and terminology in view; the OCA history itself comments on Western influences in its language.

overview.text: Spener’s Pia Desideria proposed reform within Lutheran church life through Scripture, practical Christianity, pastoral formation, and spiritual renewal. Pietism was a renewal current within Protestantism rather than the founding of one new denomination.

readings.title: Spener and the publication of Pia Desideria

overview.text: Particular Baptists first published this confession anonymously in 1677 and publicly endorsed it in 1689. It follows Westminster and Savoy extensively while requiring a profession of repentance and faith for baptism and prescribing immersion.

readings.title: Chapter XXIX.2: the subjects of baptism
readings.locator: Second London Baptist Confession XXIX.2; Schaff’s Baptist Confession of 1688/1689 section
readings.text: Those who do actually profess repentance towards God, faith in and obedience to our Lord Jesus, are the only proper subjects of this ordinance.

readings.title: Chapter XXIX.4: immersion
readings.text: Immersion, or dipping of the person in water, is necessary to the due administration of this ordinance.

overview.text: Nonjuror Anglicans begin discussions with representatives of the Patriarchate of Alexandria visiting London. This concerns a group separated from the established Church of England, rather than an agreement by all Anglicans.

readings.title: OCA history: the later Nonjuror discussions

events.title: Peter the Great replaces the Russian patriarchate

overview.text: Peter I’s Ecclesiastical Regulation replaces patriarchal government with a Holy Governing Synod under imperial oversight. The Russian patriarchate is restored by the council of 1917–1918.

readings.title: OCA history: the Holy Governing Synod

developments.text: The OCA history connects this restructuring with Protestant state-church models. It describes an administrative transformation within the Russian Church, not a conversion of that Church into a Protestant denomination.

overview.text: The Herrnhut community’s renewal is commemorated on August 13, 1727. The Unity of the Brethren originated in 1457; the renewed Moravian church therefore has a pre-Lutheran ancestry as well as eighteenth-century influence on Protestant revival.

Revival preaching associated with Jonathan Edwards, George Whitefield, and others crossed colonial denominational boundaries. The awakening generated support and opposition within existing churches; it did not produce one uniform theology or denomination.

readings.title: Revival, controversies, and New England context
readings.locator: Joseph Bellamy, Edwards, Whitefield, and the Great Awakening

overview.text: John Wesley’s experience at a London religious society became a defining memory of Methodist renewal. Wesley remained an Anglican priest; this event did not itself establish a separate Methodist denomination.

readings.title: Methodism’s Anglican and Moravian connections
readings.locator: The roots of the United Methodist family tree

overview.text: Wesleyan societies and field preaching expanded a renewal movement within the Church of England. Methodist organization gradually acquired structures that could continue outside Anglican oversight, particularly in the new United States.

events.title: Publication of the Greek Philokalia

overview.text: Makarios of Corinth and Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain compile patristic writings on the spiritual life. The first Greek edition appears in Venice in 1782, within a wider renewal of Orthodox ascetic and hesychast teaching.

events.rulingLabel: Philokalia of the Holy Neptic Fathers

readings.title: Read the original Greek first edition
OCA history: Makarios, Nikodemos, and the Kollyvades

overview.text: The Christmas Conference organized the Methodist Episcopal Church in Baltimore. The new American church gave institutional form to a movement that had originated within Anglicanism, in circumstances changed by the American Revolution.

readings.title: The Christmas Conference and the new church

overview.text: Russian monastic missionaries arrive on Kodiak Island. Their work includes Saint Herman of Alaska, whose care for Native people becomes a central part of Orthodox memory in North America.

readings.title: OCA history: the mission and Saint Herman

overview.text: The Cane Ridge meeting in Kentucky brought large crowds and multiple Protestant participants together. Barton W. Stone’s involvement became a formative context for the later Stone-Campbell movement; the revival itself did not create every Restoration church.

readings.title: Stone, Cane Ridge, and subsequent developments

events.title: Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery

overview.text: Stone and colleagues dissolved their short-lived Springfield Presbytery and appealed for Christian unity beyond sectarian names and structures. This became an important text for the Stone wing of the Restoration movement.

events.rulingLabel: Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery

readings.title: The Springfield Presbytery and Stone’s movement
Date and place in Disciples history

overview.text: The Stone and Campbell movements joined in Kentucky. The union is commonly dated 1832; the Disciples’ chronology records the representative handshake on December 31, 1831. Later Christian Churches, Churches of Christ, and Disciples developed within this broader family.

The Southern Baptist Convention formed in a sectional division involving slaveholding and missions. Its 1995 resolution acknowledged slavery’s central role in the founding and repented of racism; these institutional origins are distinct from the seventeenth-century beginnings of Baptist theology.

readings.title: The convention’s own acknowledgment of its origins

overview.text: Eastern patriarchs and their synods respond to Pope Pius IX’s invitation to union. Their encyclical disputes papal claims and the Filioque, while emphasizing the Church’s shared responsibility to preserve the received faith.

readings.title: The body of the Church
readings.text: the protector of religion is the very body of the Church, even the people themselves

events.title: Vatican I defines papal jurisdiction and infallibility

overview.text: Pastor Aeternus defined Roman primacy and papal infallibility when the pope defines faith or morals ex cathedra for the universal Church. The conditions matter: the definition does not describe every papal remark as infallible. The text presents this as a Catholic dogmatic definition.

readings.title: The specified conditions for ex cathedra definitions
readings.locator: Pastor Aeternus, chapter IV, definition; Schaff vol.II, pp.270–271, English column
readings.text: Therefore faithfully adhering to the tradition received from the beginning of the Christian faith, for the glory of God our Saviour, the exaltation of the Catholic religion, and the salvation of Christian people, the sacred Council approving, we teach and define that it is a dogma divinely revealed: that the Roman Pontiff, when he speaks ex cathedra, that is, when in discharge of the office of pastor and doctor of all Christians, by virtue of his supreme Apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine regarding faith or morals to be held by the universal Church, by the divine assistance promised to him in blessed Peter, is possessed of that infallibility with which the divine Redeemer willed that his Church should be endowed for defining doctrine regarding faith or morals; and that therefore such definitions of the Roman Pontiff are irreformable of themselves, and not from the consent of the Church.

overview.text: The Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles became a major center of the emerging Pentecostal movement. Earlier events at Topeka in 1901 also figure in its history; Pentecostalism subsequently developed several doctrinal and organizational streams.

readings.title: Early Pentecostal origins and Azusa Street

developments.text: Holiness and revival currents contributed to Pentecostal origins. The Assemblies of God is one Pentecostal fellowship; it should not be used as the name for all Pentecostal churches.

overview.text: Pentecostal ministers and believers met in Hot Springs, Arkansas, and organized the Assemblies of God. The fellowship grew within the wider Pentecostal movement; its organization was not the beginning of all Pentecostal Christianity.

The All-Russian Council restores patriarchal government. Tikhon is elected Patriarch on 5/18 November 1917, as revolution and persecution transform Russian church life. The paired date distinguishes Julian and Gregorian calendars.

readings.title: OCA History and Archives: Tikhon’s election and the council

events.title: Formation of the Russian Church Abroad

overview.text: Russian bishops establish provisional administration in southern Russia in 1919. After evacuation, their administration operates abroad, including in Sremski Karlovtsy in 1921, and develops into the Synod of Russian Orthodox Bishops Abroad.

events.rulingLabel: Provisional administration and the Synod of Bishops Abroad

readings.title: ROCOR diocesan history: evacuation and the Administration Abroad

overview.text: Patriarch Tikhon and the Russian Church’s governing bodies provide emergency arrangements for dioceses cut off from central administration. Neighboring bishops are to organize regional authority, with subsequent confirmation when central authority resumes.

developments.text: ROCOR’s official diocesan history identifies this decree as a canonical charter for the further work of the exiled church administration.

overview.text: The Confessional Synod at Barmen adopted a six-thesis declaration against the subordination of Christian proclamation and church order to rival authorities. Its immediate setting was the German church struggle under National Socialism, rather than a new Protestant denomination.

readings.title: Thesis 1: opening affirmation
readings.text: Jesus Christ, as he is attested for us in holy scripture, is the one Word of God

events.title: Vatican II: ecumenism and religious liberty

overview.text: Vatican II’s decree on ecumenism described restoration of Christian unity as a principal concern and discussed Eastern churches separately from Western Reformation communities. Dignitatis Humanae affirmed religious freedom from coercion. These documents mark later Catholic developments relevant to reading sixteenth-century controversy today.

readings.title: The council’s stated ecumenical concern
readings.text: The restoration of unity among all Christians is one of the principal concerns of the Second Vatican Council.

readings.title: Read the distinctions concerning East and West
Religious freedom
readings.text: This Vatican Council declares that the human person has a right to religious freedom.

readings.title: Read the account of freedom from coercion

events.title: Rome and Constantinople remove the 1054 censures

overview.text: Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras with his synod remove the 1054 excommunications from memory. Their joint declaration explicitly acknowledges that substantial differences remain; this act does not restore full communion.

Congregations separating from the Presbyterian Church in the United States organized the PCA at its first General Assembly. The PCA is a modern Presbyterian body in the Westminster tradition, not a church that separated directly from Eastern Orthodoxy.

readings.title: Records of the first General Assembly
The longer American Presbyterian history
readings.locator: PCUSA, the 1861 southern division, and PCUS

developments.text: The historical route runs through Western Christianity, Reformed and Scottish Presbyterian developments, and American Presbyterian divisions. A modern PCA–Orthodox comparison is theological; it is not the story of a direct institutional split.

events.title: John Piper begins pastoral ministry at Bethlehem

overview.text: Piper began serving Bethlehem Baptist Church in Minneapolis in 1980. His influence is an example of contemporary Reformed evangelical teaching within a Baptist setting; he is a teacher, not the founder of a denomination or a PCA minister.

readings.title: The ministry’s stated beliefs
readings.locator: Sections 3, 7–9, and 12: election, redemption, justification, and baptism

developments.text: Shared Reformed language does not erase the difference between Presbyterian infant baptism and Baptist believers’ baptism. Piper and the PCA should be studied as distinct contemporary reference points, not as a single lineage from Orthodoxy.

events.title: Joint Declaration on justification

overview.text: The Lutheran World Federation and the Roman Catholic Church signed the Joint Declaration in Augsburg. It reports a consensus on basic truths of justification while addressing remaining differences; its signatories do not represent every Protestant church.

events.rulingLabel: Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification

readings.title: The declaration and its institutional publication
readings.locator: Signed October 31, 1999; read the qualifications as well as the consensus

events.title: Act of Canonical Communion: Moscow and ROCOR

overview.text: The Act restores canonical communion between the Moscow Patriarchate and the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia. It specifies ROCOR’s continuing self-government in pastoral, educational, administrative, property, and civil matters.

readings.title: Read the Act of Canonical Communion

events.title: WCRC associates with the justification declaration

overview.text: The World Communion of Reformed Churches associated itself with the Joint Declaration on justification at Wittenberg. This is an ecumenical action of that communion, not a claim that all Reformed churches adopted an identical statement or entered institutional union.

events.rulingLabel: WCRC association with the Joint Declaration

readings.title: Read the underlying declaration
readings.locator: Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification

book.verifiedCoverage: Verified access is limited to a publicly available 23-page 2015 excerpt containing front matter, a table of contents, Bishop Basil’s foreword, and Trenham’s introduction (printed pp.1–9), plus official Ancient Faith interview pages/recordings. The complete book and the user’s paperback edition were not accessed. The 2015 excerpt’s table of contents runs to an index on p.391; the current publisher listing describes a 272-page edition, so excerpt page locators must not be assumed to match the paperback. Notes below summarize only verified introduction passages, not all chapters. No official interview transcript was available; interviews are linked for listening without transcript-derived claims.

notes.title: Trenham’s stated purposes
notes.text: Trenham states three purposes: a history of Protestant traditions using their own words and confessions, an account of Orthodox–Protestant relations, and an Orthodox theological appraisal. His introduction explicitly aims to avoid misrepresentation and caricature.
notes.reason: Necessary attribution of the author’s stated method

notes.title: Separation and failed reunion
notes.text: Trenham argues that centuries of separation, the sack of Constantinople, failed reunion councils, and mutual ignorance hindered contact between Orthodox leaders and Western reformers. This is his introductory interpretation of the background to the Reformation.
notes.reason: Necessary attribution of the author’s historical interpretation

notes.title: Trenham’s critique of the medieval West
notes.text: Trenham criticizes theology’s detachment from ascetic life, bishops’ political power, and papal innovations supported by forged documents. This is an Orthodox assessment in his introduction; the timeline’s primary readings separately document particular texts and decisions.
notes.reason: Necessary attribution of the author’s theological assessment

notes.title: Papal innovations
notes.text: papal innovations – theological and practical – abounded.

notes.title: Political support for reform
notes.text: Trenham emphasizes territorial rulers’ fiscal and political interests, alongside conciliarist opposition to papal authority, in the Reformation’s survival. The note identifies his causal emphasis without treating it as the sole historical explanation.
notes.reason: Necessary attribution of the author’s causal interpretation
